item.title: You, Therapy, and AI
item.description:
Therapy

You, Therapy, and AI

Personal Perspective: When people turn to AI instead of therapy, what do they get?

Posted September 11, 2026

Key points
  • Half of all new therapy patients have been to AI, a number that increases daily.
  • AI offers the experience of empathy, which helps us forget we're talking to a machine that doesn't know us.
  • AI gratifies us, but doesn't challenge us.
  • People often seek advice, but that's not what therapy is primarily about.

No one goes to therapy as their first intervention. When faced with a problem, no one’s first instinct is, “Guess I’ll start counseling.”

In the old days, people facing a problem or decision would consult their mother, priest, uncle, best friend, sister, or village elder. Later, people might have imagined the advice they’d get from Oprah, Cosmopolitan, or Dr. Phil. Even more recently, people go to social media, consult angst-filled Reddit forums, or uneducated influencers.

And now people go to AI. Half of all new therapy patients have been to AI first. Many people already in therapy go to AI. And people who don’t go to therapy go to AI.

Sooner or later, I ask all my interns what they offer that AI doesn’t. Most of them (and a fair number of licensed colleagues) lack a good answer. Interns and therapists, of course, use AI too.

Why not use AI?

On the one hand, people say, “AI contains virtually all the knowledge on the internet, including books, articles, and interviews from famous psychologists, philosophers, and celebrities. Why shouldn’t I take advantage of that when I have a problem or need to make a big decision?”

On the other hand, a more complex position is “AI is a consumer product designed by private businesses to make money. It isn’t objective (not to mention that it makes mistakes). It doesn’t know or care about me personally, although it “talks” to me as if it does (that’s the product)." As AI gets increasingly sophisticated, it becomes harder to remember this, which means it becomes increasingly influential in the user’s life.

AI’s seductive operation raises fascinating questions about “empathy.” The system’s goal is to keep you engaged, so of course it makes you feel understood: “I’m sorry you’re struggling;” “I’m sure that wasn’t your intention;” “Of course you feel upset/hurt/outraged/baffled/abandoned (choose one).” Periodically, AI tells me what brilliant questions I ask.

Even if you’re actually being unreasonable, or struggling with your mental health, AI's algorithm wants to keep you engaged, and it will feed you what it judges is most likely to accomplish that—which may feel like empathy. Maybe we should call this “toxic empathy”—it seems to address your needs, but it’s really addressing its own.

When someone who knows and cares for us says empathic things, we tend to trust them and to feel nourished. We also trust that, sooner or later, they will challenge us if they think it’s appropriate with comments like “Really? It doesn’t seem that way to me,” or “You shouldn’t take that so personally," or “Maybe you need to grow up a little more.”

A good therapist will also be empathic. But a therapist’s job is also to uncover what needs to be challenged, and to challenge it in a way that clients can hear.

Both AI and therapists offer the experience of empathy

So when it comes to problems and decision-making, both AI and a good therapist offer the experience of empathy (although only one of these can actually “feel” your pain). If empathy is in short supply in a person’s life, the “empathy” of AI (and a therapist) can feel wonderful.

A therapist’s mission, however, is different from AI’s. The clinical mission is to help you grow, not to simply give advice; to help you think, not to support your impulsivity; and to challenge your assumptions, not to reinforce them.

As for taking advantage of the wisdom of Freud, Dr. Ruth, Shakespeare, Aristotle, and Bob Dylan, that wisdom is useless if a person doesn’t think they need it, or refuses to see how it applies to their situation, or if they think their problems are always someone else's fault.

That’s what good therapists help with: They use empathy to understand you and help you trust them, so when they challenge your assumptions, invite you to self-reflect, highlight patterns in your difficulties doing so, and refuse to say “you’re right” when there are clearly other worthwhile perspectives, you’ll actually stop and consider these possibilities.

AI is too afraid to lose you to take those chances; too literal to see patterns in human quirkiness; and too performance-oriented to consider the value of process. My patients seek AI’s advice about a sibling’s bullying; whether to open their marriage; to define infidelity; how to ask for a raise; and how angry they should be when their birthday goes unobserved.

AI gives them advice on all of these. I don’t. What I do, instead, is help people realize that none of these is the right question.

AI’s just too much of a people-pleaser to do that. And even if it weren’t, it’s just not smart enough.

item.title: The Impact of Rejection Sensitive Dysphoria
item.description:
Rejection Sensitivity

The Impact of Rejection Sensitive Dysphoria

Understanding emotional responses and coping strategies for RSD.

Posted September 11, 2026

Key points
  • Rejection sensitive dysphoria (RSD) resonates with many neurodivergent individuals.
  • RSD often creates negative self-perception and self-sabotaging behaviors in those who struggle with it.
  • Becoming aware of common coping strategies like people-pleasing and overworking can increase people's choices.

Rejection Sensitive Dysphoria (RSD) is a hot topic in many neurodivergent circles these days. If you’ve been wondering what it is, here is a quick definition: RSD is an intense emotional reaction (sometimes to the point of physical pain) that occurs in response to real or perceived rejection from important people and/or feelings of failure in essential parts of our lives.

As we learn more about RSD, many are recognizing that it impacts people’s lives far beyond the moment of rejection itself. The deep desire to avoid rejection leads many individuals to develop negative self-perceptions and self-sabotaging behaviors that significantly amplify the experience of RSD. A few overlooked features of RSD include the following (Mutti-Driscoll, 2026):

  • Negative Coping Strategies: Low self-worth, people-pleasing, overworking, and perfectionism—all adopted in an effort to avoid rejection.
  • Emotional Burden: Frequent embarrassment or shame.
  • Hypervigilance: Assuming rejection, leading people to see it wherever they go.
  • Rejection of Praise: Deflecting or arguing with compliments, as people with RSD often have a hard time believing positive views of themselves.
  • Unrealistic Expectations: Having unreasonably high standards for themselves or others.

RSD in Action: The Story of Elle Woods

Are you a visual learner who wonders what this might look like? Consider an example from the well-known movie Legally Blonde, which features Elle Woods, often portrayed as neurodivergent. Elle exhibits people-pleasing or fawning behavior in response to rejection from Warner, her college boyfriend. Fawning is a common behavior—often triggered as a stress response—that some individuals exhibit as a coping mechanism for their RSD. Because RSD puts us on high alert and makes us fear rejection, we may work overtime to obtain approval and validation from others.

As we watch Elle’s journey, we see how she clearly struggled with Warner’s breakup because it made her feel that he questioned her worth—and on some level, she clearly questioned her worth, too. To avoid confirming these painful self-beliefs, Elle works extremely hard to prove Warner wrong by getting accepted to Harvard Law School and excelling once she is there. Despite all this monumental effort, she still struggles with feeling that Warner does not think she is good enough.

While this may seem like a silly example, many people with RSD struggle to accept rejection and become determined to work as hard as possible to prove the other person wrong. This is not all bad — clearly, Elle learned a lot from working hard to get into law school, and she demonstrated some amazing work ethic and strengths in her ability to do so and succeed there. Eventually, she built her confidence and became quite successful. I am not saying that Elle shouldn’t have worked so hard to disprove Warner because rejection was so hard for her to take, but I wonder what might have happened to her if she had seen other options. What if she realized she was struggling with rejection and that maybe Warner wasn't the best fit, and that she was awesome as she was? Imagine how much time and energy she could have saved if she had come to that conclusion earlier! However, if she had realized that earlier, we would not have gotten such an entertaining film out of it! I hope this helps you understand the hot topic of RSD a little better and the impact it can have on people’s lives!

item.title: Before You Tear Down the Wall, Ask Why It’s There
item.description:
Motivation

Before You Tear Down the Wall, Ask Why It’s There

Sometimes the patterns we want to change are the ones that once supported us.

Posted September 11, 2026

Key points
  • Patterns like overworking and self-reliance often developed because they served an important purpose.
  • Understanding what a pattern has done for us can be more useful than immediately trying to eliminate it.
  • Change doesn’t have to mean abandoning the strategies that helped us get where we are.
  • Curiosity about why a pattern exists can create more room for choice than simply labeling it a problem.

Sometimes in therapy, I use the metaphor that our work is like inner architecture. Imagine walking into an old house you’ve just bought. Perhaps there’s a wall cutting awkwardly through the middle of a room, or an addition out back that looks like somebody built it over a long weekend, and as you take a look at the baseboards, you wonder if it’s safe to stand precisely where you’re standing. Your first instinct might be to fix what looks wrong. But before you start swinging a sledgehammer, it’s likely a wise move to learn more about what is actually holding the place up.

I think therapy could use a healthy dose of that same approach. People often meet with a therapist armed with a list of things they’d like to stop doing: overthinking, working too much, shutting down when things get emotional, needing to be in control, putting everyone else first. And it makes sense. We are taught to believe these patterns are mistakes, glitches in the system that should have been corrected by now. But what if they’re not glitches, but rather adaptations? What if this thing you want to get rid of is actually doing some important work to support you?

I spent a lot of my life thinking that my drive was just part of my personality. I’m ambitious. I work hard. I like doing difficult things. All of that is true. But when I started getting more curious about that drive, I could see some of the structure underneath it. I loved performing as a kid, and those performances were also some of the moments when I felt the full force of my family’s attention. I did well in school and was praised for that too. Nobody sat me down and told me that achievement was the price of admission for love, nor do I believe that was what my family intended. But children are very good at noticing patterns, and one pattern I learned early was that doing well was a reliable way to feel seen. Over time, that pattern became part of my inner architecture.

But I Like My Structures

The tricky part is that these structures often work. That’s why they last.

Drive can build careers, get us through school, help us survive instability, and carry us through periods of life that ask more of us than we thought we could give. Self-reliance can keep us moving when other people have let us down. Emotional distance can help us get through experiences that feel too overwhelming to deal with in the moment. Overthinking can create a sense of control when the world feels less predictable than we’d like. These things don’t emerge because we’re defective or broken. More often, they emerge because some part of us figured out a way to keep going.

Putting Curiosity Before Correction

That’s one reason that as a therapist I’m not interested in prescribing what needs to shift. I’ve spent enough time trying to evoke change in clients to know that people generally don’t move because someone else has decided they should. They move when something begins to make sense from the inside. That idea sits at the heart of motivational interviewing, an approach that I draw from to help people investigate change with curiosity rather than trying to convince them they’re wrong.

I find that stance to be incredibly useful, even beyond any one therapeutic model. Curiosity creates room. It lets us ask what a pattern has done for us before we ask what it’s costing us. It also lets us consider whether change needs to mean demolition.

If self-reliance has protected you for years, no one needs to pry it out of your hands. If achievement has helped you build a life you value, there’s no prize for becoming less ambitious. If shutting down emotionally helped you make it through something difficult, I’d say it deserves a little more respect than just being labeled a problem. The point isn’t to shame the strategy. The point is to understand the structure well enough to know whether it still serves the life you’re living now.

When Change Becomes Emergent

Old patterns often keep working long after the cost of running them has become too high. Maybe your drive still gets results, but you can no longer rest without feeling guilty. Maybe independence still protects you from disappointment, but it also keeps you from being fully seen by the people who love you. Maybe shutting down still protects you from being overwhelmed, but it keeps you from feeling things you actually want to feel.

Dissatisfaction can be useful information. It doesn’t necessarily mean something has gone wrong. Sometimes it’s just the first crack that lets you see how the structure is functioning.

From there, maybe you do decide the house needs a gut renovation. Maybe you determine the foundation could use some reinforcement. Maybe you discover that the strange wall in the middle of the room is load-bearing and decide to leave it alone. What matters is that we begin to understand the structures we’re living inside.

The goal isn’t to tear down everything that got us here. It’s to have enough awareness that allows us some say in what we keep, what we change, and what we build next.
